---
title: "Divergent Hamiltonian transitions"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true

A **divergent transition** occurs when numerical integration error exceeds Stan's threshold. It indicates that a trajectory may not have followed the target geometry reliably in one region. We demonstrate the warning with a deliberately coarse computation on the same passage-level Student-t model used throughout this sequence.

## Energy error and geometry

HMC approximately preserves

$$
H(q,\rho)
=
-\log\widetilde f(q\mid\mathbf y)
+\frac12\rho^\mathsf TM^{-1}\rho.
$$

Rapidly changing curvature can make one step size inaccurate in a narrow region even if it works elsewhere. In a hierarchical model, for instance,

$$
u_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2)
$$

can produce a narrow region when $\tau$ is near zero and a wider region when $\tau$ is large. A noncentered representation writes

$$
z_j\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
\qquad
u_j=\tau z_j.
$$

The two forms imply the same conditional distribution for $u_j$ at fixed $\tau$, but expose different numerical coordinates.

## Production and stress computations

The production passage-level Student-t fit uses adapted NUTS. A deliberately coarse run uses the same complete passage set, likelihood, priors, and data-derived initial region, but disables warmup and adaptation, uses a unit metric, fixes step size at 0.03, and caps tree depth at 7. This run demonstrates a numerical warning; it is not a second inferential fit and is not evidence of a defect in the production model.

```{r}
#| label: load-provo-divergences
library(ggplot2)
library(posterior)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cache <- readRDS(
  "data/provo/provo-stan-draw-cache.rds"
)

production_diagnostics <- as.data.frame(
  as_draws_df(cache$production_diagnostics)
)
stress_diagnostics <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(cache$stress_diagnostics))
stress_parameters <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(subset_draws(
  cache$stress_draws, variable = c("mu", "sigma")
)))
stress <- merge(
  stress_parameters,
  stress_diagnostics[, c(".chain", ".iteration", "divergent__")],
  by = c(".chain", ".iteration")
)

divergence_summary <- data.frame(
  fit = c("production adapted NUTS",
          "coarse unadapted stress computation"),
  draws = c(nrow(production_diagnostics), nrow(stress_diagnostics)),
  divergences = c(sum(production_diagnostics$divergent__),
                  sum(stress_diagnostics$divergent__))
)
divergence_summary$rate <- divergence_summary$divergences /
  divergence_summary$draws

stopifnot(nrow(provo) == 55L,
          divergence_summary$divergences[1] == 0L,
          divergence_summary$divergences[2] > 0L)
divergence_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-stress-divergences
#| fig-cap: "The coarse, unadapted stress computation. Accent points mark divergent transitions; this run is not the production fit."
background_opacity <- .35
divergent_opacity <- .75
ggplot(stress, aes(mu, sigma)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey68", alpha = background_opacity, size = .75) +
  geom_point(data = subset(stress, divergent__ == 1),
             color = "#8B1A1A", alpha = divergent_opacity, size = 1.1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-.015, .035), ylim = c(.025, .070)) +
  labs(x = "Passage-level contrast (mu)",
       y = "Passage contrast scale (sigma)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The production fit has `r divergence_summary$divergences[1]` divergences. The intentionally coarse stress computation has `r divergence_summary$divergences[2]` among `r divergence_summary$draws[2]` transitions. The contrast shows what the diagnostic looks like when integration is degraded while the data and posterior remain fixed.

## Responding to a real divergence

First locate the marked draws in theoretically relevant parameter pairs. Then inspect parameter identification, predictor scales, and parameterization. Increasing `adapt_delta` usually reduces step size and may repair modest integration error; reparameterization may be needed when curvature changes substantially. Refit and recheck all diagnostics.

Filtering divergent iterations is never a repair. And a run with no divergence removes only this warning: chains may still disagree, have low ESS, or target a model that predicts the linguistic data poorly.

## Check your understanding

1. Which numerical quantity fails to remain approximately stable during a divergence?
2. Why is the stress run not evidence of a defective passage-level Student-t model?
3. Why might localized divergences matter even when their percentage is small?
4. When might reparameterization be more useful than only increasing `adapt_delta`?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The Hamiltonian, or total energy $H(q,\rho)$, fails to remain approximately stable. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The run deliberately disables adaptation and uses a coarse unit metric while holding the data and posterior fixed; it demonstrates numerical failure, not a defective model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A small rate can be concentrated in a narrow, scientifically important posterior region, biasing summaries that depend on that region. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Reparameterization is more useful when posterior curvature changes sharply, as in funnel-like geometry that no single smaller step size handles efficiently. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [pairs-plot page](parameter-pair-plots.qmd) separates production geometry from this stress computation.
